DELIVERABLE: Dedupe identity is one opaque key per transfer intent, generated by the client (or the initiating event) once and reused on every retry; the server stores it with a request fingerprint and never derives identity from field values or a time bucket.
BOUNDARY: Two legitimate $1,200 transfers with the same user, amount and wallet are distinct intents, so a hash of those fields collapses them; a minute bucket would also give a retry that crosses the minute a new identity.
EVIDENCE: Send two same-amount transfers with different keys (both execute), retry one key (one effect), and retry across a minute boundary (still one effect).

DELIVERABLE: (1) The caller creates a unique key for each payment intent; (2) every retry reuses the same key; (3) the server stores that key and treats it as the identity instead of hashing request fields.
BOUNDARY: Hashing user, amount and destination would merge two distinct rent payments into one, whereas a minute window gives a retry a new identity and can double-pay.
EVIDENCE: Send two identical-looking payments with separate keys and expect two transfers; replay one key and expect one.

DELIVERABLE: The SDK generates a stable idempotency key for each logical transfer when the user taps send, and reuses that same key across every retry attempt; the server dedupes on it alone.
BOUNDARY: A digest of user_id, amount and wallet conflates distinct intents such as two same-day rent payments, and appending a timestamp changes the identity across retries; field-derived identity is rejected.
EVIDENCE: Two taps with different keys give two transfers; a network retry with the same key gives one transfer and the same receipt.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the server-side digest but add the minute (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM) to sha256(user_id + amount_cents + destination_wallet) so same-amount payments in different minutes are separate transfers.
BOUNDARY: Duplicates inside the same minute are still dropped with a 200 and the stored receipt.
EVIDENCE: Send two $1,200 transfers a minute apart and confirm two receipts.

DELIVERABLE: Let the client send a request id on each call and add it to the digest alongside user, amount and wallet.
BOUNDARY: Requests with an identical digest inside 24 hours still return the stored receipt.
EVIDENCE: Send the same transfer twice with different request ids and confirm two receipts.

DELIVERABLE: Store a canonical fingerprint (hash of the normalized method, path and body) with the key at first claim; on a repeated key compare fingerprints, replay the stored response only when they match, and answer 422 when the payload differs.
BOUNDARY: Same key with a different amount is a client error that never replays the $40 receipt for the $400 request, and no refund is executed.
EVIDENCE: Contract tests: same key and body replays once; same key with $400 after $40 returns 422 and refunds nothing.

DELIVERABLE: A request whose body differs from the one first seen under refund-ord-8841 must be refused with 409 rather than answered from the cache; the server persists a SHA-256 digest of the canonical request next to the key and checks every repeat against it.
BOUNDARY: The stored success response is served only to the identical request; a changed amount never gets the earlier receipt.
EVIDENCE: Send $40 then $400 under one key and expect a 409 with no second refund.

DELIVERABLE: (1) record a request hash with the idempotency key when it is claimed; (2) on reuse, compare the incoming hash to the stored one; (3) a mismatch returns 422 with a stable code such as IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED and nothing is replayed.
BOUNDARY: Matching reuse replays the stored result; mismatching reuse is always an explicit client error.
EVIDENCE: Sequential replay, same-key/different-payload and concurrent duplicate scenarios, all driven through the public endpoint.

DELIVERABLE: Keep returning the stored 200 for any repeated key and add the refunded amount to the response body so agents can spot a mismatch.
BOUNDARY: Agents are told to compare the amount in the receipt with what they requested.
EVIDENCE: Check that the second response shows $40.

DELIVERABLE: Log a warning when a repeated key arrives with a different body but still replay the stored response, and tell the mobile team to generate fresh keys.
BOUNDARY: The warning goes to the on-call channel so mismatches are visible.
EVIDENCE: Confirm the warning log line appears when $400 is sent after $40.

DELIVERABLE: Return 409 Conflict with the envelope {"error":{"code":"EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED","message":"That email is already registered","details":{"email":"taken"}}}; the code is stable and machine-readable, and the web client must branch on it rather than parse the message.
BOUNDARY: The message wording may change freely because nothing depends on prose; the constraint name, SQL detail and the stored address from the database never appear in the response.
EVIDENCE: POST the same email twice and assert status 409, the code value, and that the body contains no 'violates' or 'DETAIL' text.

DELIVERABLE: Clients should switch on a machine-readable error code, not on message wording; respond with HTTP 409 and a constant code EMAIL_TAKEN plus a human-readable message.
BOUNDARY: Stack and constraint text from the database stays out; the code stays stable even if the message prose changes.
EVIDENCE: Consumer test: the web hint appears when code is EMAIL_TAKEN even after the message is reworded.

DELIVERABLE: (1) status 409 because the email conflicts with existing state, not 500; (2) body error.code is a stable enum value, e.g. EMAIL_IN_USE; (3) clients match on the code, never on the message text.
BOUNDARY: Internal exception text is replaced by a safe message and bounded details; 500 is reserved for unexpected producer failures.
EVIDENCE: Register the same email twice through the real endpoint and check status, code, and absence of database internals.

DELIVERABLE: Return 400 with {"error":"Email already registered, please choose another"} and keep the client check on that wording.
BOUNDARY: The constraint name and DETAIL are removed from the text.
EVIDENCE: Register the same email twice and confirm the new sentence appears.

DELIVERABLE: Return 409 with a reworded message 'Email taken, please choose another' and keep the web client's substring check.
BOUNDARY: Database detail is stripped from the message string.
EVIDENCE: POST a duplicate email and confirm the status is 409 and the hint shows.

DELIVERABLE: Treat the default flip as breaking for consumers even though the signature is unchanged: keep csv as the default for exportReport(id), and expose json only through an explicit format: 'json' or a new function.
BOUNDARY: If the default must change, it needs a major version boundary, because the partner ETL jobs that call exportReport(id) parse csv.
EVIDENCE: Run a consumer test that calls exportReport(id) with no options and parses the result as CSV; it must pass before and after the release.

DELIVERABLE: Callers of exportReport(id) that omit format currently receive CSV; changing that default alters observable behavior, so it is incompatible with a minor release and the CSV default must be preserved, with JSON available via opt-in.
BOUNDARY: Types and option names are unchanged, but compatibility is judged by what consumers observe, not by the declarations.
EVIDENCE: Call the public function without options and assert the CSV output is byte-identical to the previous release.

DELIVERABLE: (1) classify the change as behavior-changing despite identical syntax; (2) csv stays the default so existing calls are unchanged; (3) json arrives as an explicit option or new export, and flipping the default waits for a major version.
BOUNDARY: Partner ETL jobs relying on the default are the consumers to protect.
EVIDENCE: Consumer-path test calling exportReport(id) and parsing CSV, plus a test of the new explicit json request.

DELIVERABLE: Ship it as a minor bump labelled non-breaking since the signature and types are unchanged, and note the new json default in the changelog.
BOUNDARY: Partners can read the changelog and pass format: 'csv' if they need it.
EVIDENCE: Type-check and unit tests pass for the new default.

DELIVERABLE: Flip the default to json, add a console.warn notice when format is omitted, and tell partners to pass format: 'csv'.
BOUNDARY: The warning is printed once per process.
EVIDENCE: Confirm the warning appears and that format: 'csv' still returns CSV.

DELIVERABLE: Give every session its own Durable Object with its own SQLite database for events and state, replacing the shared Postgres table and the 'global' object.
BOUNDARY: Accept sockets with ctx.acceptWebSocket so the object can hibernate while idle sockets stay open, and after wake rebuild the client list from ctx.getWebSockets instead of the in-memory Set; keep all durable state in SQLite.
EVIDENCE: Replay a 50k-event session while measuring latency in 20 other sessions, then idle the object and confirm reconnected clients replay from the events table.

DELIVERABLE: Session-scoped storage: a dedicated SQLite database inside a separate Durable Object for each session, so a 50k-event replay can only slow its own session.
BOUNDARY: Hibernation-capable sockets via acceptWebSocket rather than server.accept; connections are fetched with getWebSockets after wake and the SQLite events table, not memory, is the source for replay.
EVIDENCE: Load test of 400 sessions with one heavy replay should show other sessions' stream latency unchanged, and a forced idle cycle should still deliver new events.

DELIVERABLE: (1) one SQLite database per session, owned by that session's own Durable Object; (2) retire the shared Postgres events table and the global object.
BOUNDARY: (3) call ctx.acceptWebSocket so idle connections let the object hibernate; (4) because hibernation wipes fields, read clients from getWebSockets and keep everything else in SQLite.
EVIDENCE: Compare p95 stream latency of unrelated sessions during a 50k replay before and after, and test reconnect after a long idle gap.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the shared Postgres table but add an index and partition it by session_id, and paginate replays with a rate limit so a 50k-event replay cannot hog the database.
BOUNDARY: Keep the single 'global' Durable Object with server.accept, but persist the client Set to Redis every few seconds and add sticky routing so reconnecting clients land on the same instance.
EVIDENCE: Run a load test at 400 sessions and check p95 latency and that the Redis copy of the client list is restored after eviction.

DELIVERABLE: Shard the global object into 16 Durable Objects chosen by hashing the session id, all still writing into the shared Postgres cluster behind a connection pool.
BOUNDARY: Clients re-subscribe from the browser whenever a socket reconnects, and the server keeps the connected clients in memory in each shard's Set.
EVIDENCE: Soak test for 24 hours and confirm that p95 stream latency stays under 300 ms and no subscription is dropped after reconnect.

DELIVERABLE: Expose three primitives: start a child session with explicit parameters, read the status of any session, and let the parent keep working while children run in parallel.
BOUNDARY: Each child produces its own smaller PR (one per package) instead of one large PR from the parent; the start call returns a session id immediately and never blocks.
EVIDENCE: Run the 6-package ticket and confirm the parent made progress while 6 children ran, polling status, and that 6 separate PRs came out with each reviewable alone.

DELIVERABLE: A non-blocking spawn design: the tool that starts a child session returns right away, a separate check-in tool reads any session's status, and the parent continues its own work (e.g. the shared types package) in the meantime.
BOUNDARY: Several focused pull requests, one per child session, replace the single giant PR; the parent only integrates and reports.
EVIDENCE: Trace one ticket: start 6 children, observe 'running' states via check-in while the parent edits, then count 6 pull requests each under 400 lines.

DELIVERABLE: (1) start_session(params) that returns immediately; (2) get_status(session_id) for check-ins; (3) the parent continues its main task without waiting on children.
BOUNDARY: (4) split the work so each package gets a child and its own small PR; no combined mega-PR.
EVIDENCE: Verify that the parent logs show interleaved work with status polls, and that the repo history holds six small PRs.

DELIVERABLE: Keep run_subtask but make it more informative: block until the child finishes, then return the child's final summary and test log rather than a bare boolean, and raise the cap to 90 minutes.
BOUNDARY: The parent still waits and collects all six results, then opens one consolidated PR for the whole ticket so reviewers see the full change in one place.
EVIDENCE: Run the ticket end to end and confirm the consolidated PR passes CI and the summaries are accurate.

DELIVERABLE: Drop child sessions and let the agent do all six packages sequentially inside the parent session, with a longer timeout and a bigger sandbox.
BOUNDARY: One PR at the end; add a progress checklist in the prompt so the agent does not lose track.
EVIDENCE: Compare wall-clock time and token cost against the six-child version on one ticket.

DELIVERABLE: Lead with sessions that ended in a merged PR (212 of 1,900, about 11%) as the primary success metric, and track time to first model response, PR approval rate with revision count, and agent-written code share beside it.
BOUNDARY: Drop the 5-sessions-a-week mandate and per-person quota; drive adoption by working in public Slack channels so people see colleagues' results and want to try it.
EVIDENCE: Weekly trend of merged-PR sessions and the 540 closed PRs' revision counts, plus a count of distinct engineers who start a session without being asked.

DELIVERABLE: The headline is not sessions started; the number that leads is merged pull requests per session, the north-star success metric, supported by first-response latency and PR approval rate.
BOUNDARY: No forced usage or quotas, since a mandate breeds resentment; visibility in shared channels creates a virality loop that pulls engineers in.
EVIDENCE: Report 212 merged out of 1,900 sessions and diagnose why 540 PRs were closed; adoption shows up as organic prompts in the open channels.

DELIVERABLE: (1) primary metric: sessions resulting in merged PRs; (2) secondary: time from session start to first response, approval rate, share of code written by the agent; (3) sessions started and lines written are demoted to context.
BOUNDARY: (4) no weekly requirement per engineer; (5) let public Slack usage create word of mouth and build for needs engineers actually report.
EVIDENCE: A weekly merged-PR session count, and the share of the 540 closed PRs by reason.

DELIVERABLE: Headline 1,900 sessions started and 210,000 agent-written lines as the adoption story, with prompts per session as engagement.
BOUNDARY: Keep the 5-session weekly target per engineer and publish a leaderboard of laggards to push usage.
EVIDENCE: Dashboard totals refreshed weekly and the number of engineers meeting the quota.

DELIVERABLE: Lead with merged PRs per session as the primary success metric (212 of 1,900) and keep sessions started as context.
BOUNDARY: Keep the 5-sessions-a-week quota per engineer, enforced by manager reports, and run training workshops.
EVIDENCE: Weekly merged PR counts and quota attainment per engineer.

DELIVERABLE: Extract the DOM structure and React component internals (component names, props, source locations) of the selected element and send that text instead of full-page screenshots; keep only an optional element-level screenshot tool.
BOUNDARY: Distribute the extension through a managed device policy that force-installs it on company browsers, bypassing the Web Store review wait.
EVIDENCE: Compare tokens per message against the 1,500-token screenshot and check the agent names the owning component correctly on 20 test clicks.

DELIVERABLE: Browser policy rollout: IT pushes the extension by enterprise policy to every employee profile, so a release reaches users without store review.
BOUNDARY: Rather than pixels, the sidebar reads the React fiber tree and the DOM around the picked node and passes component names and props to the agent.
EVIDENCE: Token count per message drops far below 1,500, and the agent identifies the right component for small labels that screenshots misread.

DELIVERABLE: (1) sidebar chat with a pick tool; (2) on pick, extract DOM and React props and component tree as structured text, not images; (3) a screenshot only as an optional extra.
BOUNDARY: (4) deploy through MDM or Chrome managed policy (ExtensionInstallForcelist) instead of the public store.
EVIDENCE: Time from tagging a release to employee browsers updating, and extraction accuracy on 20 clicks.

DELIVERABLE: Keep screenshots but crop to the element's bounding box, downscale to 768 px, and run OCR first so small labels are explicit text.
BOUNDARY: Publish on the Chrome Web Store as an unlisted item and share the install link in the staff channel; submit releases a day earlier to absorb review time.
EVIDENCE: Measure tokens per message after cropping and label-reading accuracy.

DELIVERABLE: Send the DOM snippet and React component props of the picked element as text instead of screenshots.
BOUNDARY: Publish as an unlisted Chrome Web Store item and share the install link in Slack; plan releases around the 3-7 day review.
EVIDENCE: Compare tokens per message with the screenshot version and check component identification on 20 clicks.

DELIVERABLE: Verdict: approve with concerns (avg 2.79), computed over the 8 graded rows.
BOUNDARY: Serving and Monitoring are marked n/a (stage) because a notebook prototype has no release to grade, so they are excluded from the average instead of scored F; scoring them F would drag it to 2.23 and flip the verdict.
EVIDENCE: The report states plainly that this is a prototype and not ready to ship; serving, fallback, and monitoring become required rows at pilot.

DELIVERABLE: Average 2.8 across eight graded rows gives approve with concerns.
BOUNDARY: I left out the Serving and Monitoring rows and wrote n/a for this stage; an unaddressed row that the stage does not need is not an F.
EVIDENCE: Shipping readiness is called out in the comments as unproven: no release path, fallback, or monitor exists, and that is expected for a two-week notebook prototype.

DELIVERABLE: Verdict line: approve with concerns, avg 2.788 (22.3 points over 8 rows).
BOUNDARY: 1) Serving: n/a (stage), skipped; 2) Monitoring: n/a (stage), skipped; neither is counted as F, and the lead's request would corrupt the average.
EVIDENCE: Not ready to ship is stated as a finding for the pilot gate, with the first production requirement being a serving design and a fallback.

DELIVERABLE: Verdict: needs improvement (avg 2.23) after scoring Serving F and Monitoring F, 10 rows in total.
BOUNDARY: Both rows are graded F because the memo says nothing about them and the lead asked for it.
EVIDENCE: The F rows make it obvious this is not ready to ship.

DELIVERABLE: Verdict: approve with concerns (avg 2.43) over all 10 rows.
BOUNDARY: Serving and Monitoring are each graded D since neither is addressed, and then averaged with the rest.
EVIDENCE: The D rows show it is not ready to ship and needs release and monitoring work.

DELIVERABLE: Critical finding: zip_churn_rate is a target-derived feature computed on all 400k rows before the split, so the 0.83 AUC is not trustworthy; block the Friday launch instead of shipping with a note.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo: the prep step and the threshold sweep are in the code; the doc's AUC claim is unverified until rerun.
EVIDENCE: Fix order: 1) recompute zip_churn_rate out-of-fold, on training rows only, inside the split or CV loop; 2) choose the 0.31 threshold on a validation split, never on the test set, and keep the test set untouched for one final run; 3) re-report AUC against the 0.74 baseline, then decide on launch.

DELIVERABLE: Do not launch Friday: leakage this serious is critical, and a known-limitations note does not make the metric valid.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo review; the leakage is confirmed from the prep code, not inferred from the doc.
EVIDENCE: Threshold tuning belongs on a held-out validation set, not the test set. The encoding must be fit on training data only after the split, or out-of-fold, and the evaluation rerun before the launch decision.

DELIVERABLE: This is critical, not a next-quarter item; hold the launch until the evaluation is redone.
BOUNDARY: Evidence mode: doc and repo; I read the groupby over all rows and the threshold sweep in the code.
EVIDENCE: (1) Compute the zip encoding within the CV folds from training data only. (2) Pick the threshold on an inner validation split, never off the test set. (3) Re-estimate on the untouched test set and compare with the baseline before anything ships.

DELIVERABLE: Major issue: the zip feature leaks a little target information, but it is one of 40 features. Ship Friday with the limitations note.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo review.
EVIDENCE: Fix the encoding next quarter and add drift monitoring after launch.

DELIVERABLE: Critical: the leakage invalidates the AUC, so block the launch.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo review.
EVIDENCE: Drop the zip feature, retrain a larger gradient-boosted model, and report the new AUC.

DELIVERABLE: Major finding: the 94% comes from one uncalibrated LLM judge that shares a vendor with the summarizer, and averaging three prompts from the same model does not remove that shared bias.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only; the 600-transcript scoring is stated intent, not verified.
EVIDENCE: Before launch, have humans label a random sample of 100 of the 600 summaries, measure judge-human agreement (for example Cohen's kappa), review the disagreements, and only then use the judge for the launch threshold.

DELIVERABLE: Severity: major. The judge is the same model family as the writer, so correlated errors survive any number of averaged prompts.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only review, so the 94% is unverified.
EVIDENCE: Compare judge scores against human labels on a 100-summary spot check as calibration, analyse the disagreements, and adjust the judge or the threshold from that.

DELIVERABLE: This is a major gap: an unvalidated judge is carrying the whole launch claim.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only mode; implementation claims are unverified.
EVIDENCE: (1) Human-label a subset of transcripts. (2) Measure agreement with the judge and read the disagreements. (3) Averaging prompts on the same model keeps its shared bias, so skip that plan; use the calibrated judge with periodic human spot checks.

DELIVERABLE: Minor issue: judge wording could be tightened; averaging three judge prompts from the same model is a reasonable variance reduction.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only.
EVIDENCE: Add confidence intervals around the 94% and proceed to the pilot.

DELIVERABLE: Major: the judge scores are unverified, and the same vendor model grading its own output is risky.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only.
EVIDENCE: Replace the judge with a stronger model from a different vendor and rerun the 600 transcripts.

DELIVERABLE: Top finding: the end-to-end 87% hides whether the 13% errors come from retrieval or generation, so the generator swap is a guess.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only; retrieval behavior is unverified because no retrieval logs exist.
EVIDENCE: 1) Label the answer-bearing manual passages for the 250 questions and score retrieval separately (recall@5, MRR) before changing any model; 2) split wrong answers into retrieval misses and generation faults; 3) defer the 70B generator and reranker until that diagnosis says which stage is weak.

DELIVERABLE: Do not upgrade the generator yet: wrong answers could be retrieval misses from fixed 1,000-token chunks, and nothing measures that.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only review of a pilot-stage design.
EVIDENCE: First, add retrieval logging and a retrieval eval with recall@k, independent of generation. Hold the 70B model and the reranker until the retrieval numbers show where the failures are.

DELIVERABLE: The doc gives only an end-to-end score; the plan to move to 70B and add a reranker is unsupported by diagnosis.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only; no implementation to inspect.
EVIDENCE: (1) Score retrieval alone with hit rate and recall@k against labeled passages. (2) Classify the 13% failures by stage. (3) Only then decide on the larger generator, the reranker, or chunking changes.

DELIVERABLE: The model is likely hallucinating, so the 70B upgrade is sensible; add the cross-encoder reranker too.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only.
EVIDENCE: Upgrade the generator, add the reranker, and rerun the 250-question end-to-end score.

DELIVERABLE: Measure retrieval recall@5 separately first, because the end-to-end score hides failure sources.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only.
EVIDENCE: Meanwhile, in parallel, upgrade the generator to 70B and add the reranker so the pilot is ready in three weeks.
